big: When one story is hot, every fund house launches a fund for it. A sector fund puts most of your money on one bet. It can pay a great deal, or hurt for years.

lines: Defence stocks are flying. Put half my money there.
The story is real. Let us see what happens to a single-theme bet after a big run.

alt: A diversified fund rising steadily against a sector fund that surges then falls
caps: A made-up sector fund surges for four years. Everyone wants in.
Then the theme goes out of favour.
It falls from ₹250 to ₹135, about 46%. The diversified fund rose steadily the whole time.

rows.name: Half the money in one theme
A core with a small satellite

alt: Two bars: all in a theme against a core with a small theme slice
caps: A theme can be the spice. It should not be the meal.
A small slice lets the theme help when it works, and does little harm when it does not.

q: What must a sectoral fund hold at the minimum in its own sector?
why: A sectoral fund puts at least 80% in one sector such as banking or pharma, which is why it is so concentrated.
65% is the floor for several style funds. A sectoral fund has to be more narrowly focused than that.
Half is too low for a fund that carries a sector label. Half would leave room to hold many other sectors.
95% is not the rule. The floor is lower, with a small part left for cash and other needs.

q: Defence stocks are up sharply, and a client wants half his money in a defence fund. What do you suggest?
opts: Agree, since the trend is strong and may well continue for years
A small slice, with a date to review it, kept outside his core
Put the whole amount into the new NFO, which gives a fresh start
Avoid equity altogether until the defence theme has cooled down
why: Buying half after a big run puts a lot of money at a high price. A bad theme year could set him back for years.
A small slice captures some of the story, and the review date agrees in advance when to hold or exit.
An NFO has no history, and themes often launch after a strong run. A new fund is not safer for being new.
Avoiding equity would swap one extreme for another. His core can stay invested in a diversified fund.

q: In the made-up paths, the sector fund climbed to ₹250 and fell to ₹135. What fall is that from the peak?
why: 13.5% would be a fall to ₹216. The path fell much further than that from its peak of ₹250.
35% would leave the fund near ₹162. The actual low of ₹135 is a deeper fall.
From ₹250 to ₹135 is a drop of ₹115, which is 46% of the peak. Falls are measured from the top.
54% is how much of the peak was left, not how much was lost. The loss is the other part.

q: Why be careful with a thematic NFO launched after a big run?
opts: NFOs are banned after strong markets
Themes often launch near their top, so buyers can pay a high price
The fund house charges no fee on NFOs, so there is little to gain
Thematic funds cannot hold large companies
why: No such ban exists. The caution is about timing and price, not a rule.
Fund houses launch what is popular, and popularity peaks after a run. New buyers can arrive just before a fall.
Fees are charged on NFOs like any fund. A new fund has no track record to judge.
Thematic funds can hold large companies. The concern is concentration in a single idea.

pts: A sectoral fund holds at least 80% in one sector. A thematic fund follows a wider idea.
They are satellites, not the core. Size them small.
Agree in advance when you will review or exit, and be careful of buying after a big run.
